kasparov.name: Garry Kasparov
kasparov.title: 13th World Champion (1985–2000)
kasparov.bio: Born in Baku. At 22 he took the title from Anatoly Karpov and held it for 15 years until losing to Vladimir Kramnik in 2000. He was the world's top-rated player for almost twenty years and retired in 2005.
kasparov.style: A dynamic attacking player who valued the initiative above material. He arrived with deep opening preparation and often decided the game before the opponent found their bearings.

carlsen.name: Magnus Carlsen
carlsen.title: 16th World Champion (2013–2023)
carlsen.bio: A Norwegian who became a grandmaster at 13. He won the title from Viswanathan Anand in 2013 and held it until 2023, when he chose not to defend it. He reached the highest rating in history, 2882.
carlsen.style: A universal player. He happily enters equal positions and keeps pressing, squeezing wins out of tiny advantages. Strongest in endgames and practical decisions at the board.
strengths: Playing on with a tiny edge

fischer.name: Bobby Fischer
fischer.title: 11th World Champion (1972–1975)
fischer.bio: An American who won the US championship at 14. In Reykjavik in 1972 he beat Boris Spassky, ending the Soviet hold on the title. In 1975 he refused to defend it, and the crown passed to Anatoly Karpov.
fischer.style: Clarity and precision. He played clean classical positions, almost always opened with 1.e4 and converted even small advantages. He fought in every game and disliked quick draws.

karpov.name: Anatoly Karpov
karpov.title: 12th World Champion (1975–1985)
karpov.bio: Became World Champion in 1975 when Fischer declined to defend the title. He defended the crown twice against Viktor Korchnoi and was the world's best for a decade until losing to Garry Kasparov. He later held the FIDE title again (1993–1999).
karpov.style: A master of positional play. He slowly squeezed opponents, taking away space and useful moves, and then won with almost no risk. His style is often compared to a boa constrictor.

capablanca.name: José Raúl Capablanca
capablanca.title: 3rd World Champion (1921–1927)
capablanca.bio: A Cuban prodigy who learned chess as a small child by watching his father play. He won the title from Emanuel Lasker in 1921 and lost it to Alexander Alekhine in 1927.
capablanca.style: Simplicity and clarity. Capablanca avoided needless complications, played lightly and precisely, and handled endgames so well that his games are still studied as models.

tal.name: Mikhail Tal
tal.title: 8th World Champion (1960–1961)
tal.bio: "The Magician from Riga". In 1960 he beat Mikhail Botvinnik to become World Champion and lost the rematch a year later. Despite poor health he stayed among the world's elite for decades.
tal.style: The most dazzling attacking player in history. He sacrificed pieces to complicate the position and won in the chaos, where opponents could not calculate everything.

botvinnik.name: Mikhail Botvinnik
botvinnik.title: 6th World Champion (1948–1963, with breaks)
botvinnik.bio: Won the 1948 match-tournament to become World Champion. He lost the title twice, to Smyslov and Tal, and won it back both times in rematches. An engineer by training, he later ran a chess school whose pupils included Karpov, Kasparov and Kramnik.
botvinnik.style: A scientific approach. He prepared meticulously, analysed his own games and openings in depth, and played logically and powerfully in complex strategic positions.

alekhine.name: Alexander Alekhine
alekhine.title: 4th World Champion (1927–1935, 1937–1946)
alekhine.bio: In 1927 he sensationally beat Capablanca. He lost the title to Max Euwe in 1935 but regained it two years later. He died in 1946 as the reigning champion, the only one in history.
alekhine.style: An attacking style built on deep combinations. Alekhine could create complications out of nothing and calculated many moves ahead.

morphy.name: Paul Morphy
morphy.title: The unofficial world's best in the late 1850s
morphy.bio: An American from New Orleans. In 1858–1859 he toured Europe and beat its strongest masters, including Adolf Anderssen. Soon after returning home he all but gave up chess.
morphy.style: Rapid development, open lines and attack. Morphy was the first to show consistently how important it is to mobilise every piece before attacking.

lasker.name: Emanuel Lasker
lasker.title: 2nd World Champion (1894–1921)
lasker.bio: A German player and mathematician. He beat Steinitz in 1894 and held the title for 27 years — the longest reign in history — until losing to Capablanca in 1921.
lasker.style: A practical fighter. Lasker looked not for the perfect move but for the one most uncomfortable for the specific opponent, and he defended difficult positions brilliantly.

spassky.name: Boris Spassky
spassky.title: 10th World Champion (1969–1972)
spassky.bio: Beat Tigran Petrosian in 1969. In 1972 in Reykjavik he lost the famous "Match of the Century" to Bobby Fischer.
spassky.style: A universal player. Equally confident in attack and defence, he played sharp openings like the King's Gambit and manoeuvred calmly in level positions.

petrosian.name: Tigran Petrosian
petrosian.title: 9th World Champion (1963–1969)
petrosian.bio: Beat Botvinnik in 1963 and defended the title against Spassky in 1966, before losing the 1969 rematch to him. Nicknamed "Iron Tigran" for his incredibly solid play.
petrosian.style: A master of prophylaxis who foresaw and neutralised the opponent's plans in advance. Famous for positional exchange sacrifices that players still study.

kramnik.name: Vladimir Kramnik
kramnik.title: 14th World Champion (2000–2007)
kramnik.bio: In London in 2000 he sensationally beat Garry Kasparov without losing a game. In 2006 he unified the title by beating Veselin Topalov and passed the crown to Anand in 2007. He retired in 2019.
kramnik.style: Deep positional understanding and flawless preparation. In the match against Kasparov he made the Berlin Defence popular, and the whole elite took it up afterwards.

anand.name: Viswanathan Anand
anand.title: 15th World Champion (2007–2013)
anand.bio: India's first grandmaster (1988). FIDE World Champion in 2000 and undisputed champion from 2007 until he lost the 2013 match to Magnus Carlsen.
anand.style: Fast and universal. Known for lightning calculation and deep opening preparation, equally at home in sharp and quiet positions.

polgar.name: Judit Polgár
polgar.title: The strongest female player in history
polgar.bio: A Hungarian who became a grandmaster in 1991 at 15 years and 4 months, breaking Fischer's record. The only woman to reach the world top ten (8th, 2004) and to pass a 2700 rating. She retired in 2014.
polgar.style: An aggressive attacking style. Polgár readily sharpened the game and sacrificed material to steer it into tactical battles, where she was especially strong.

smyslov.name: Vasily Smyslov
smyslov.title: 7th World Champion (1957–1958)
smyslov.bio: Played three title matches against Botvinnik, winning in 1957 but losing the rematch a year later. He stayed at the top for decades and reached the Candidates final in 1984 at the age of 63.
smyslov.style: Harmony and naturalness. Smyslov placed his pieces as if they knew where they belonged, and he was renowned for his endgame skill.

steinitz.name: Wilhelm Steinitz
steinitz.title: 1st official World Champion (1886–1894)
steinitz.bio: Born in Prague. In 1886 he beat Johannes Zukertort in the first official World Championship match and held the title until 1894, when he lost to Emanuel Lasker.
steinitz.style: The father of positional chess. Steinitz formulated the principles of accumulating small advantages and showed that an attack must be justified by the position, not just by daring.

short.name: Nigel Short
short.title: World title challenger (1993)
short.bio: An Englishman and one of the strongest Western players of the 1980s and 90s. In 1993 he played a world title match against Garry Kasparov and lost.
short.style: Aggressive and inventive. Unafraid of unusual ideas, like his famous king march across the board against Jan Timman.

byrne-fischer-1956.title: "The Game of the Century"
byrne-fischer-1956.why: 13-year-old Fischer against Donald Byrne in New York. The queen sacrifice 17…Be6 and the rout that followed made the whole chess world notice Fischer.

kasparov-topalov-1999.title: Kasparov's Immortal
kasparov-topalov-1999.why: Wijk aan Zee, 1999. The rook sacrifice 24.Rxd4 and a hunt for the black king across the whole board. One of the most beautiful attacks in chess history.

fischer-spassky-1972-g6.title: Match of the Century, game 6
fischer-spassky-1972-g6.why: Reykjavik, 1972. Fischer, who almost always opened 1.e4, started with 1.c4 and outplayed Spassky in classical style. The win put him ahead in the title match.

karpov-kasparov-1985-g16.title: The knight on d3
karpov-kasparov-1985-g16.why: The 1985 world title match. Kasparov's knight on d3 paralysed the whole white army — one of the best-known games of their rivalry. Kasparov became champion that year.

short-timman-1991.title: The King March
short-timman-1991.why: Tilburg, 1991. In the middlegame Short marched his king Kh2–g3–f4–g5 into the enemy camp to join the attack on the black king.

carlsen-karjakin-2016-tb4.title: Title tiebreak, 2016
carlsen-karjakin-2016-tb4.why: New York, 2016, the final tiebreak game. On his birthday Carlsen finished it with the queen sacrifice 50.Qh6+ and kept his world title.

tal-larsen-1965-g10.title: The decider in Bled
tal-larsen-1965-g10.why: The Candidates semifinal in Bled. The score before this game was 4.5–4.5. Tal sacrificed a knight with 16.Nd5, won and reached the Candidates final.

aronian-anand-2013.title: A 23-move demolition
aronian-anand-2013.why: Wijk aan Zee, 2013. Reigning champion Anand, with Black, crushed Aronian in 23 moves with a series of sacrifices — one of the finest games of his career.

carlsen-anand-2013-g5.title: Title match 2013, game 5
carlsen-anand-2013-g5.why: Chennai, 2013. After four draws Carlsen won the first game of the match, grinding Anand down in the endgame. The match made him World Champion.

carlsen-karjakin-2016-g10.title: Title match 2016, game 10
carlsen-karjakin-2016-g10.why: New York, 2016. Karjakin led the match after game 8. In game 10 Carlsen levelled the score after a long fight, and the match eventually went to a tiebreak.

morphy-opera-1858.title: The Opera Game
morphy-opera-1858.why: Paris, 1858, in a box at the opera. Morphy played the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, who consulted each other. The queen sacrifice 16.Qb8+ and mate with 17.Rd8# make it the most famous short game in chess history and a model of rapid development.

lasker-bauer-1889.title: The double bishop sacrifice
lasker-bauer-1889.why: Amsterdam, 1889. Lasker sacrificed both bishops — 15.Bxh7+ and 17.Bxg7 — and tore open the black king's shelter. The idea has been known as Lasker's double bishop sacrifice ever since.

botvinnik-capablanca-1938.title: The bishop on a3
botvinnik-capablanca-1938.why: The AVRO tournament, 1938. The young Botvinnik outplayed former World Champion Capablanca and finished the game with the famous bishop sacrifice 30.Ba3.

spassky-bronstein-1960.title: The James Bond game
spassky-bronstein-1960.why: USSR Championship, Leningrad, 1960. The King's Gambit, the knight sacrifice 16.Nxf7 and an attack on the king. A position from this game appears at the start of the James Bond film "From Russia with Love" (1963).

steinitz-bardeleben-1895.title: Hastings, 1895
steinitz-bardeleben-1895.why: The veteran Steinitz against Curt von Bardeleben. After 22.Rxe7+ the white rook keeps checking and cannot be taken. Von Bardeleben did not wait for the mate and simply left the tournament hall.

capablanca-marshall-1918.title: The birth of the Marshall Attack
capablanca-marshall-1918.why: New York, 1918. Frank Marshall surprised Capablanca with a new, sharp pawn sacrifice 8…d5 in the Ruy Lopez. Capablanca beat off the attack and won, yet the idea is still called the Marshall Attack and is played at the highest level.

kramnik-kasparov-2000-g2.title: London 2000, game 2
kramnik-kasparov-2000-g2.why: The World Championship match. Kramnik's first win over Kasparov. Kramnik won the whole match without losing a single game and became the 14th World Champion.

reti-alekhine-1925.title: The Baden-Baden combination
reti-alekhine-1925.why: Baden-Baden, 1925. With Black, Alekhine played one of his most famous combinations, calculated many moves ahead, against Richard Réti, one of the fathers of the hypermodern school.

karpov-unzicker-1974.title: The boa constrictor in Nice
karpov-unzicker-1974.why: The Nice Olympiad, 1974. A textbook example of Karpov's style: step by step he took away his opponent's space and useful moves until Black was completely squeezed.

store.title: Guess the Grandmaster's Move
store.short: Play through world champions' games and guess their moves. 108 legendary games.
store.full:
Can you think like a grandmaster?

In this game you don't play against a computer — you guess the moves that great champions made in real games. Choose Kasparov, Carlsen, Fischer, Tal or any of 18 grandmasters and replay their most famous games move by move.

• 108 real games: from Morphy's 1858 Opera Game to 21st-century world championship matches
• Every move is evaluated by a chess engine: even if you don't match the master but find an equally strong move, you score points
• Profiles of 18 champions: biography, playing style, strengths
• Move of the day — one position a day, the same for everyone
• GM index: how close your thinking is to each grandmaster
• Colour themes, board colours, sound and game pace
• Works offline

Learn to think like the champions — one move at a time.
